text:
The new MCP and OAuth surface held up on every probe, and nothing is exploitable without a household login. I found one medium DoS risk (not tested live), two low issues, and one deviation from your brief. The one client I registered is `hm_client_oJJtgjNRNFk0kJy1ngpS2LQ78HQerSiwJ8BGsx4irr4`.

**Deviation from your brief:** the server refused `https://example.com/cb`, because redirect hosts are allowlisted (claude.ai, claude.com, chatgpt.com, googleusercontent). I registered once with `https://claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callback` instead (201).

**Findings, most severe first**

1. **Medium: registration DoS (code read, not exercised live).**
   - `src/app/api/oauth/register/route.ts` rate-limits per `clientAddress(req)`.
   - `clientAddress` in `src/core/net/rate-limit.ts:32` trusts a client-supplied `x-real-ip` first. If the Railway edge doesn't overwrite it, a spoofed header bypasses the per-IP limit of 10 per hour.
   - The global cap of 30 per day and `MAX_CLIENTS=50` still hold. Even without the spoof, an attacker can use up the 30 per day and block real Claude or ChatGPT registrations.
   - Fix: take the address only from the proxy-set header (the rightmost trusted `x-forwarded-for` hop), and consider a per-day cap that doesn't let one source fill it.

2. **Low: cookies on public, cacheable responses.**
   - `curl -si $H/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` returns `cache-control: public, max-age=3600` together with `set-cookie: __Host-authjs.csrf-token=…` and `__Secure-authjs.callback-url=…`.
   - This applies to the well-known documents and the OPTIONS responses.
   - A shared cache could store a Set-Cookie. Fix: don't let the proxy attach Auth.js cookies to these paths.

3. **Low: `OPTIONS /api/mcp` gets a 204 with no `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers.**
   - The same request on `/api/oauth/token`, `/register` and `/.well-known/*` returns `access-control-allow-origin: *` with methods GET, POST, OPTIONS.
   - `*` is fine here, since the token and register endpoints take no cookies. A browser-based MCP client would be blocked on `/api/mcp`. Probably intended; confirm.

4. **Info: the error body reflects the submitted redirect URI.**
   - The 400 from `/api/oauth/register` echoes it back (up to 200 characters) as JSON, which is harmless.
   - The huge `client_name` case was not sent, to avoid creating a record. The code sanitises it and caps it at 80 characters.

**Checks that passed**
- **Discovery documents (1):** the issuer and resource are fixed to the production origin (`…/api/mcp`), and `code_challenge_methods_supported` is `["S256"]`. The `/api/mcp` suffix variant works.
- **`/api/mcp` (2):** the status is 401 for no token, a garbage Bearer, GET and POST. The header is `www-authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", resource_metadata=".../.well-known/oauth-protected-resource", scope="household:read"`. The body is a generic `invalid_token`, with no stack trace.
- **Registration validation (3):** `javascript:`, `http://evil.com`, `myapp://`, `https://claude.ai.evil.com`, userinfo in the URL, port 8443, missing `redirect_uris` and non-JSON all return 400. Per `isAllowedRedirectUri`, `http://localhost` and `http://127.0.0.1` on any port or path would be accepted. That is by design (RFC 8252) and was not sent.
- **`/oauth/authorize` unauthenticated (4):** every variant gets a 307 to `/signin?callbackUrl=<relative path>`. That covers plain, a missing challenge, a mismatched redirect, an unknown client and CRLF in `state`. There is no open redirect and no header injection. The client, redirect and PKCE checks run only after sign-in, with an exact-match redirect and S256 enforced (`authorize.ts:36-50`).
- **Token and revoke (5):** error bodies are clean JSON (`invalid_grant`, `unsupported_grant_type`). GET returns 405. Revoke with a bogus token returns 200, which RFC 7009 allows.
- **Path tricks (6):** `/api/mcp/../finance`, `/.well-known/../api/finance`, `/api/oauthx`, `/api/oauth` and `/api/oauth/foo` all return 401. `/oauth/authorizeX` and `/.well-known/foo` redirect to signin. The public-path matching is exact or `p + "/"`, so no extra routes opened.
- **Security headers (7):** the CSP, HSTS, `x-frame-options: DENY`, nosniff and `referrer-policy` headers are present on all of these routes.

The progress note is at `/data/workspaces/runs/rmwqgwchc88f8c8/.agent-notes/security-prober.md`. The registration response is saved in the scratch folder as `reg.txt`.

  ## Findings
  Nothing above MINOR. All three fix commits hold up.
  
  - [C1] MINOR - Path traversal does not get around the 50f9472 matcher exclusion. Next runs the matcher on `parsedUrl.pathname`, which comes from WHATWG `new URL`, and runs it a second time on the decoded path (`node_modules/next/dist/server/lib/router-utils/resolve-routes.js:342-351`). I checked the parser with node:
    - `/.well-known/../finance`, `/.well-known/%2e%2e/finance` and `/.well-known/.%2e/finance` all become `/finance`, so the proxy runs.
    - `/.well-known/..%2ffinance` is left as is, so the proxy is skipped. But the router doesn't turn it into `/finance`: it 404s, or lands in the public `[[...path]]` discovery handlers.
    - `next.config` `headers()` still sends CSP and frame-ancestors on these paths, because it doesn't depend on the proxy.
  
    The gap: `tests/proxy-matcher.test.ts` only tests the regex, not traversal or encoded paths. I couldn't confirm any of this against a running server: my scratch Next app wouldn't start because Turbopack kept resolving the parent repo. So it rests on reading the source.
  - [C2] MINOR - The refresh endpoint only reads `client_id` from the form body (`src/app/api/oauth/token/route.ts:28`) and never looks at an HTTP Basic `Authorization` header. Registration forces `token_endpoint_auth_method: "none"` (`server.ts:68`), so clients that follow the spec send it in the body; the MCP SDK does. If ChatGPT or Gemini leave it out, their refresh now fails with `invalid_request`. That is a compatibility risk I could not verify. A Basic-header fallback costs little.
  - [C3] MINOR - When `redirect_uri` is missing, the code is consumed before the check (`server.ts:155-161`) and the error is `invalid_grant` instead of `invalid_request`. This is safe; it only affects how clear the error is.
  
  ## Prior findings (your rankings)
  - Refresh M: I'd lower it to L now that 294947e is in. Refresh tokens still aren't rotated and still slide within 90 days (`server.ts:202`), so rotation is still worth adding.
  - Registration DoS L: agree. Even with an honest IP, the per-IP limit is 10/h (`register/route.ts:16`), so one attacker hits the 30/day global cap in 3 hours. Spoofable `x-real-ip` (`rate-limit.ts:33`) only makes it quicker. Unused clients are pruned after 24h (`server.ts:79`), so the effect is limited to availability.
  - Any path on an allowed host accepted as redirect_uri, L: agree. The attack only works if the assistant's callback `state` isn't tied to the session that started the flow.
  - PNR leak: I'd raise it to the top L. It directly contradicts `docs/SECURITY.md:99`, and booking codes are useful to an attacker.
  - Info items: agree. Also: any `http://localhost:*` port is accepted (`policy.ts:88`), which is fine for public clients.
